title: Functor infinity categories turn source pushouts into pullbacks
statement:
Use quasicategories, coherent functor categories, full subcategories and mapping spaces as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. Fix a universe of small quasicategories and a larger universe for their collection $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$. This infinity category has small colimits and is cartesian closed, with internal Hom the quasicategory $\operatorname{Fun}(A,E)$ including all coherent natural transformations. For a span of small infinity categories $B\leftarrow A\to D$ and its pushout $P=B\amalg_A D$ in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$, restriction gives an equivalence of infinity categories
$$\operatorname{Fun}(P,E)\simeq\operatorname{Fun}(B,E)\mathop{\times}^{h}_{\operatorname{Fun}(A,E)}\operatorname{Fun}(D,E)$$
for every infinity category $E$ in a sufficiently large universe. The right side is the pullback in $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$: its objects consist of functors on $B,D$ and a coherent equivalence between their restrictions to $A$; its transformations include noninvertible transformations with their coherent compatibility on $A$. These equivalences are natural in maps of spans and in $E$, and commute with composition of transformations. In particular this assertion is about the whole functor infinity category, not just its core.

source.place: Section 3.1.3, especially the internal Hom preceding Proposition 3.1.3.3; Proposition 3.1.4.2 and Corollary 3.1.4.3 for the cartesian model structure over a point; Corollary 4.2.4.8 for small colimits of the associated infinity category. The displayed internal-Hom pushout formula is an agent-formulated consequence of cartesian closedness and the mapping-space universal property. No Stacks tag states this infinity-categorical formula.

proof.text:
Realize $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ by the coherent nerve of the fibrant objects in the marked cartesian model over a point. All marked objects are cofibrant and a fibrant object is $C^
atural$ for a quasicategory $C$. Thus the model mapping Kan complex from $C^
atural$ to $D^
atural$ is $\operatorname{Fun}(C,D)^\simeq$, and the coherent-nerve comparison identifies it with $\operatorname{Map}_{\mathrm{Cat}_\infty}(C,D)$. This fixes the meaning of $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ and of its mapping spaces without invoking an ordinary homotopy category.

By [lem-coef-cat-infinity-colimits-cartesian-closure], $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ admits all small limits and colimits, including the empty ones, and coherent functor categories are its internal Homs. Its universe clause lets us form a colimit of the small input in its input universe and test its universal property after enlarging to contain $E$. Thus the pushout $P$ and the pullback $R$ below exist independently of any enriched diagram-model theorem. The actual exponential comparison and pushout-to-pullback argument are written in Steps 3--6; they retain the given cocones and all transformations.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.4.4; Theorem 4.2.4.1; Corollary 4.2.4.8, together with the universe-relative marked model construction.

proof.text:
For quasicategories $T,A,E$, the exponential identity is explicit in each simplicial degree: a map $T	imes\Delta^n	o\operatorname{Fun}(A,E)$ is a map $T	imes\Delta^n	imes A	o E$, and permuting the last two factors makes it a map $T	imes A	imes\Delta^n	o E$. This gives an isomorphism $\operatorname{Fun}(T,\operatorname{Fun}(A,E))\cong\operatorname{Fun}(T	imes A,E)$, commuting with all simplicial operators. Both sides are quasicategories. Taking cores and using the mapping-complex identity of step 1 gives $\operatorname{Map}(T,\operatorname{Fun}(A,E))\simeq\operatorname{Map}(T	imes A,E)$. Equivalences are preserved by this isomorphism; pointwise equivalence identifies the marked exponent $(E^
atural)^{A^
atural}$ with $\operatorname{Fun}(A,E)^
atural$. Products have their degreewise simplicial meaning, since their model mapping complexes are products. This proves cartesian closedness with the whole $\operatorname{Fun}(A,E)$ as internal Hom.

source.place: Internal Hom preceding Remark 3.1.3.1; Definition 3.0.0.1; the simplicial exponential identity.

proof.text:
For every $T,X$, apply step 3 and the pushout universal property to compute
$$\operatorname{Map}(T\times P,X)\simeq\operatorname{Map}(P,\operatorname{Fun}(T,X))\simeq\operatorname{Map}(B,\operatorname{Fun}(T,X))\times^h_{\operatorname{Map}(A,\operatorname{Fun}(T,X))}\operatorname{Map}(D,\operatorname{Fun}(T,X)).$$
Uncurrying the three factors identifies the last space with the coherent cocones from $T\times B\leftarrow T\times A\to T\times D$ to $X$. Thus $T\times P$ is the pushout of the product span. All these maps are restrictions or the explicit currying of step 3, so the displayed equivalence uses the canonical product cocone.

source.place: Agent deduction from the exponential identity and the mapping-space universal property of a pushout.

proof.text:
Let $R$ be the pullback of $\operatorname{Fun}(B,E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(A,E)\leftarrow\operatorname{Fun}(D,E)$; step 2 supplies it. Restriction of a diagram on $P$ and its coherent gluing along $A$ defines a comparison $\phi:\operatorname{Fun}(P,E)\to R$. For every quasicategory $T$, the pullback universal property and step 3 identify $\operatorname{Map}(T,R)$ with
$$\operatorname{Map}(T\times B,E)\times^h_{\operatorname{Map}(T\times A,E)}\operatorname{Map}(T\times D,E).$$
Step 4 identifies this space with $\operatorname{Map}(T\times P,E)$, and step 3 identifies that with $\operatorname{Map}(T,\operatorname{Fun}(P,E))$. The resulting map is exactly $\operatorname{Map}(T,\phi)$, since each factor is restriction along a leg of the given cocone.

source.place: Agent mapping-space computation using the colimit and limit universal properties; internal Hom preceding Remark 3.1.3.1.

proof.text: Write $S=\operatorname{Fun}(P,E)$. The equivalence of $\operatorname{Map}(R,\phi)$ gives $\psi:R\to S$ with $\phi\psi\simeq\mathrm{id}_R$. Since $\operatorname{Map}(S,\phi)$ is injective on components and $\phi\psi\phi\simeq\phi$, it follows that $\psi\phi\simeq\mathrm{id}_S$. These are coherent natural equivalences because the mapping spaces in step 1 are the cores of functor quasicategories. Hence $\phi$ is an equivalence of quasicategories. The argument tests all $T$, including non-groupoidal $T$, rather than just the core of $S$.

source.place: Lemma 3.1.3.2, whose inverse argument is written out here; Definition 3.0.0.1.

proof.text: For the description of the pullback, put $C=\operatorname{Fun}(A,E)$, $W=(C^\natural)^{(\Delta^1)^\sharp}$ and let $V$ be its underlying simplicial set. Apply [lem-coef-infinity-equivalence-arrow-path-object]: $V$ is the full subcategory of $\operatorname{Fun}(\Delta^1,C)$ on equivalence edges, $W=V^\natural$, and its joint endpoint map is a model fibration. This applies because $C$ is a quasicategory by [lem-cbc-enhanced-functor-cone-calculus].

source.place: HTT Sections 3.1.3–3.1.4 and Remark A.2.4.5; apply the extracted marked endpoint-fibration and sharp mapping-complex lemmas, then unfold the simplex data.

proof.text:
Set $X=\operatorname{Fun}(B,E)$, $Y=\operatorname{Fun}(D,E)$ with their restriction functors to $C$. Form $H=(X^
atural	imes Y^
atural)	imes_{C^
atural	imes C^
atural}V^
atural$ and write $R$ for its underlying simplicial set. The endpoint fibration from Step 7 satisfies the hypothesis of [lem-coef-infinity-pullback-mapping-space], so $H=R^
atural$ is fibrant and $R$ is a quasicategory. Neither restriction $X	o C$ nor $Y	o C$ is assumed to be a fibration.

source.place: HTT Sections 3.1.3–3.1.4 and Remark A.2.4.5; apply the extracted marked endpoint-fibration and sharp mapping-complex lemmas, then unfold the simplex data.

proof.text:
For every quasicategory $Q$, apply [lem-coef-infinity-pullback-mapping-space]. Its isomorphism computes $\operatorname{Map}^\sharp(Q^
atural,R^
atural)$ as the path-space homotopy pullback of the sharp mapping Kan complexes into $X^
atural,C^
atural,Y^
atural$. By the mapping-space identification of Step 1 these are the corresponding $\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$ mapping spaces. The formula preserves the given projections and interval path, so the mapping-space cone criterion proves that $R$, with this cone, is the pullback used in Step 5.

source.place: HTT Sections 3.1.3–3.1.4 and Remark A.2.4.5; apply the extracted marked endpoint-fibration and sharp mapping-complex lemmas, then unfold the simplex data.

proof.text: Unfold the degreewise marked pullback and the full-subcategory description of $V$. An $n$-simplex of $R$ consists of diagrams $B\times\Delta^n\to E$ and $D\times\Delta^n\to E$, together with a map $\Delta^n\times\Delta^1\to C$ having their restrictions as endpoints and carrying every $\{v\}\times\Delta^1$ to an equivalence. For $n=0$ this is the two functors and an equivalence between their restrictions; for $n=1$ it is their transformations with the compatible square, and higher $n$ retain its coherences. No condition is imposed that the $\Delta^n$ directions be equivalences. Thus noninvertible transformations are retained.

source.place: HTT Sections 3.1.3–3.1.4 and Remark A.2.4.5; apply the extracted marked endpoint-fibration and sharp mapping-complex lemmas, then unfold the simplex data.

proof.text: Restriction of maps $K\times\Delta^n\to E$ commutes with precomposition in $K$, postcomposition in $E$, and every simplicial operator. The currying maps only permute factors, so they have the same compatibilities. Therefore the comparison $\phi$ is natural contravariantly in maps of spans and covariantly in $E$, retaining all higher compatibility simplices. The pointwise equivalence criterion makes this natural comparison an equivalence of functor quasicategories. Composition of transformations is preserved because the comparison is a simplicial functor, restricting the very same $2$-simplices that witness composition. This proves the stated naturality and composition clauses for the full functor categories.
